newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore commodity rules aimed at shysters- trade.
newsitem.headline: Singapore commodity rules aimed at shysters- trade.

text.p: Proposed new regulations for soft commodity trading in Singapore are aimed at illegal outfits victimising gullible people, traders said on Wednesday.
Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu said on Tuesday the city-state would consider drafting laws to regulate soft commodities trading.
Hu said, when asked in Parliament, that the government is thinking of enacting such laws to stop firms who trick Singaporeans by promising them very high returns, state television reported.
"This refers more to fly-by-night commodity companies," a senior rubber dealer said. "This is not a problem for us. We are registered at the (government's) Trade Development Board."
"I believe it would be directed against people promising fantastic returns," a vegetable oil trader said.
Another rubber dealer said the illegal companies prey on Singaporeans whom they swindle out of their savings.
"The trouble does not lie with those brokers. The trouble lies with those people who are too greedy and too stupid. They're so naive, trying to make a fast buck," the dealer said.
A veteran coffee trader said the firms usually call people on the phone or canvass houses on a door-to-door basis.

"They guarantee a profit. Then they take a deposit, say (Singapore) $10,000 or $20,000, and they say they will use the funds to trade in the market. Then they come back later and they say they've lost the money," he said.
Traders said they know of several such cases where people have lost their money.
"One guy swiped $3 million. He came back and he's now sitting in jail. These are bucket-shop operators and they're still hanging around," one said.
Hu had said legislation would be used to regulate the activities of these companies, although no further details were available on the kind of laws that might be passed.
One dealer said it may be difficult to keep track of commodity traders here who set up illegal trading outfits.
"It can be done, but the expense is high. It's difficult to police all these traders," the dealer said.
Singapore has a rubber exchange and robusta coffee contracts are also traded in the prosperous city-state.
Many traders in physical grains and oilseeds, palm oil, cocoa and other commodities are also based in the country and use Singapore as the hub of their regional operations.
